Setting up a project

Source: vignettes/setup.Rmd
setup.Rmd

This article is for anyone setting weft up in a project, or taking it out again. After it you will know what each use_*() function writes and why, how to choose how weft is activated, how weft treats files it wrote that you have since edited, and how to remove each part. The last section lists every setting in _weft.yml.

The examples change files in a project, so they are not run when this article is built. Each was run in a scratch project, and the output shown is what it printed. Paths have been shortened.

One call: use_weft()

use_weft() runs every installer in order, from one plan:

Step Runs when Writes
use_setup() always _weft.yml, and the activation (a .Rprofile line or front matter)
use_quarto() in a Quarto project the weft-check extension (the filters weft.lua and weft-check.lua), the render scripts, entries in _quarto.yml
use_dictionary() always dict.yml and its schema
use_hooks() in a git work tree the commit-msg hook
use_ci() when origin is on github.com a GitHub Actions workflow
use_agent_docs() always a block in AGENTS.md and a Claude skill

It prints the plan, then writes. In a Quarto website with a GitHub remote:

weft::use_weft()
#> weft will set up creek-site:
#>   use_setup       .Rprofile (edit), _weft.yml (new), index.qmd (edit)
#>   use_quarto      _extensions/weft-check/_extension.yml (new), _extensions/weft-check/weft.lua (new), _extensions/weft-check/weftlib/ (new), _extensions/weft-check/weft-check.lua (new), _weft/pre-render.R (new), _weft/post-render.R (new), _quarto.yml (edit)
#>   use_dictionary  dict.yml (new), _weft/dict.schema.json (new)
#>   use_hooks       .git/hooks/commit-msg (new)
#>   use_ci          .github/workflows/weft.yml (new)
#>   use_agent_docs  AGENTS.md (new), .claude/skills/weft/SKILL.md (new)
#> Wrote: .Rprofile, _weft.yml, index.qmd, _extensions/weft-check/_extension.yml, ...

The call is the consent: it never asks. If any step cannot be done safely, it writes nothing and says why. If a step fails part-way, it undoes what the earlier steps wrote.

Running it again changes nothing:

weft::use_weft()
#> weft will set up creek-site:
#>   use_setup       nothing to change
#>   use_quarto      nothing to change
#>   use_dictionary  nothing to change
#>   use_hooks       nothing to change
#>   use_ci          nothing to change
#>   use_agent_docs  nothing to change
#> Nothing to change: the project is already set up.

After you update weft, run use_weft() again. It brings the files weft wrote up to date and records the new version in _weft.yml.

Every installer can also be run on its own, and each is silenced by suppressMessages().

What is in the project now: status()

status() reports each part, and the next step to take. In an R Markdown folder that has not been set up:

weft::status()
#> weft status: rmd
#>   setup        missing   no _weft.yml
#>   activation   missing   no .Rprofile line and no front-matter route
#>   quarto       n/a       not a Quarto project
#>   dictionary   missing   no dict.yml
#>   hooks        n/a       not a git repository
#>   ci           n/a       not a git repository
#>   agent docs   missing   AGENTS.md block: missing; skill: missing
#>   draft        ok        draft mode is off
#>   verify_skip  ok        verify() skips nothing
#>   strict       ok        no rule is strict
#> Next: run weft::use_setup() to write _weft.yml and record the weft version.

A part’s state is one of:

  • ok;
  • missing;
  • outdated: the file is from another version of weft, or the hook’s Rscript has gone;
  • edited: a file weft wrote has been changed by hand (see below);
  • off: draft mode is on, or verify() skips a part;
  • n/a: the part does not apply here.

status() writes nothing.

Activation: use_setup()

weft does nothing in a document until it is activated, which means weft_setup() has run before the knit reaches any prose. Loading the package with library(weft) does not activate it. use_setup() chooses one of two routes:

  • .Rprofile, the default in a Quarto project. R runs the project’s .Rprofile before every knit, so every document is covered, including one added later.
  • front matter, the default elsewhere. Each document gets the line itself, so a document copied out of the project still works.

use_setup(route = "rprofile") or use_setup(route = "front-matter") chooses for you.

The .Rprofile route

A new .Rprofile looks like this:

# weft: activates weft in every knit of this project (weft::use_setup(), rule 9.2.1).
# R reads this file instead of your ~/.Rprofile; the next line keeps yours.
if (file.exists("~/.Rprofile")) source("~/.Rprofile")
if (requireNamespace("weft", quietly = TRUE)) weft::weft_setup()

R reads only one profile, so the new file runs yours first. An existing .Rprofile gains the two weft lines at its end, after renv’s activation line, so weft is found in renv’s library:

# my profile
source("renv/activate.R")

# weft: activates weft in every knit of this project (weft::use_setup(), rule 9.2.1).
if (requireNamespace("weft", quietly = TRUE)) weft::weft_setup()

requireNamespace() means R still starts in the project for a collaborator who does not have weft. Their renders, though, do not resolve the constructs: a span prints as plain text, and an inline value that calls claim() or u() stops with “could not find function”.

The front-matter route

use_setup() in a folder of R Markdown documents edits each one:

weft::use_setup()
#> weft will write, under rmd:
#>   _weft.yml  (new: settings, and the weft version that set the project up)
#>   survey.Rmd  (edit: adds the weft setup line and names the weft-check filter)
#>   weft-check.lua  (new: the weft-check filter for rmarkdown)
#>   weft.lua  (new: the weft filter for rmarkdown)
#>   weftlib/...  (new: the modules weft.lua loads, one line each)
#> Wrote: _weft.yml, survey.Rmd, weft-check.lua, weft.lua, weftlib/...

The document’s front matter was output: html_document. It is now:

---
title: "Survey"
output:
  html_document:
    pandoc_args: ["--lua-filter", "weft.lua", "--lua-filter", "weft-check.lua"]
knitr:
  opts_knit:
    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()
---

weft-check.lua is a Pandoc filter. It reads the output after the knit and reports any construct left unresolved, such as a span whose key was misspelt. weft.lua resolves named values (see vignette("named-values", package = "weft")) and runs first; it loads its modules from weftlib/. In a Quarto project, use_quarto() installs the same filters as an extension.

Quarto documents need engine: knitr

Quarto chooses an engine for each document from the code it holds, and weft runs only under knitr. use_setup() therefore adds engine: knitr to each .qmd that names no engine, so that every document with constructs is knitted. It leaves a document that names jupyter: alone, and files and folders whose names start with _ or . (included files).

The key must be in each document’s own front matter. An engine: in _quarto.yml does not count, and the lint engine finds a document that lacks it.

When an edit is not safe

use_setup() and use_quarto() edit YAML as text, line by line, and keep every other line, comments included. When a file is written in a way they cannot edit safely, they change nothing and print the lines to add by hand:

weft::use_quarto()
#> Error: weft cannot edit _quarto.yml as text without risking what is in it, so it has changed nothing. Add these lines by hand, then run use_quarto() again:
#>
#> filters:
#>   - weft-check
#> project:
#>   pre-render: _weft/pre-render.R
#>   post-render: _weft/post-render.R
#>
#> (merge them into the `filters:` and `project:` entries the file already has; each of those holds a list, and `weft-check` and the two scripts go into it.)

This _quarto.yml had filters: [a, b] on one line.

A Quarto project: use_quarto()

use_quarto() writes three things and names them in _quarto.yml:

project:
  type: website
  pre-render:
    - _weft/pre-render.R
  post-render:
    - _weft/post-render.R
filters:
  - quarto
  - weft-check
  • _extensions/weft-check/ holds the filters weft.lua and weft-check.lua, and the folder weftlib/ that weft.lua loads.
  • _weft/pre-render.R runs before anything renders. It stops the render, naming the file, when a .qmd holds a construct and has no engine: knitr.
  • _weft/post-render.R runs after the render. It prints one report of the failures from every chapter, then fails the render if there were any. A book or website therefore reports all its failures at once, rather than stopping at the first chapter.

Both scripts are plain base R, so they run where weft is not installed.

use_quarto() stops in a folder with no _quarto.yml. It does not turn a folder into a Quarto project.

The dictionary: use_dictionary()

use_dictionary() writes dict.yml, a starter with two examples commented out, and _weft/dict.schema.json. The first line of dict.yml points an editor such as VS Code or Positron at the schema, so the editor checks each entry as you type:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=_weft/dict.schema.json

An existing dict.yml is never changed. See vignette("units", package = "weft") for the entries themselves.

The commit gate: use_hooks()

use_hooks() writes .git/hooks/commit-msg, which runs the commit gate on each commit. It needs a git work tree:

weft::use_hooks()
#> Error: use_hooks() needs a git work tree, and rmd is not in one (not a git repository). Run git init first.

The hook records the Rscript and library paths of the session that installed it. Run use_hooks() again after you upgrade R or move your library. When the repository already has a commit-msg hook from another tool, use_hooks() leaves it alone and prints the line to add to it. See vignette("gate", package = "weft").

Git does not copy hooks with a repository, so each collaborator runs use_hooks() (or use_weft()) once in their own clone.

Pull requests: use_ci()

use_ci() writes .github/workflows/weft.yml at the top of the repository. On each pull request it installs weft and runs weft::verify(static = TRUE), compared with the point where the branch left its base. It needs origin to be on github.com.

Coding agents: use_agent_docs()

use_agent_docs() tells a coding agent the rules of a weft project. It appends a block to AGENTS.md, creating the file if needed, and writes a skill to .claude/skills/weft/SKILL.md. If the project has a CLAUDE.md that does not include AGENTS.md, it says so:

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md: add the line @AGENTS.md to it, or move the block there.

vignette("agents", package = "weft") describes what the block and the skill say.

Files you have edited

Each file weft writes carries a marker: a weft-file: line, or for AGENTS.md a <!-- weft:start ... --> line. The marker holds the weft version and a hash of the file’s other lines. With it, an installer can tell three cases apart:

  • weft’s file, unedited: replaced when this version of weft would write something different;
  • weft’s file, edited by you: left as it is. status() reports it as edited, and overwrite = TRUE replaces it;
  • no marker: another author’s file. It is never replaced, even with overwrite = TRUE.
weft::use_agent_docs()
#> weft will write, under creek-site:
#>   AGENTS.md  (keep: the weft rules for coding agents)
#>   .claude/skills/weft/SKILL.md  (edited: edited since weft wrote it; left as it is (use overwrite = TRUE to replace it))
#> Nothing to change: the agent documents is already set up.

use_hooks(), use_ci() and use_agent_docs() take overwrite.

What weft writes while it works

Besides the files above, weft writes:

  • _weft/ledger/: the ledgers, one folder per source. Commit them. See vignette("gate", package = "weft").
  • .weft/: working files for a render, such as each document’s record of the checks it ran. It holds its own .gitignore, so git ignores it.
  • .git/weft/: the gate’s cache.
  • A cache of the units database, under tools::R_user_dir("weft", "cache"), outside the project.

Removing weft

To take weft out of a project, undo each part. Only the hook has a function; the rest are files to delete or lines to remove.

Part Remove
hook use_hooks(remove = TRUE), which also removes .git/weft/
activation, .Rprofile route the two # weft: and weft::weft_setup() lines in .Rprofile, or the file if weft created it
activation, front-matter route the knitr: opts_knit: weft: lines in each document
R Markdown filter weft.lua, weft-check.lua, weftlib/, and the pandoc_args line that names them
Quarto _extensions/weft-check/, _weft/pre-render.R, _weft/post-render.R, and their three entries in _quarto.yml
dictionary dict.yml and _weft/dict.schema.json
continuous integration .github/workflows/weft.yml
agent documents the block between <!-- weft:start and <!-- weft:end --> in AGENTS.md, and .claude/skills/weft/
records _weft/ledger/ and .weft/
settings _weft.yml 
weft::use_hooks(remove = TRUE)
#> weft will remove, under creek-site:
#>   .git/hooks/commit-msg  (remove: the weft commit-msg hook)
#> Removed: .git/hooks/commit-msg

Remove the constructs from the documents first, or render with weft still active. Without weft, a document that holds them prints each span as plain text, and claim() and u() are not found.

Settings

_weft.yml sits at the project root. Every key has a default, so the file holds only what you change. A document can set most of them for itself under a weft: key in its front matter:

weft:
  digits: 2

draft, decisions and verify_skip belong to the project and may only be set in _weft.yml. Never put a weft: key in _quarto.yml; the lint config-place finds one there. A misspelt key is kept, with a warning that names it.

Setting Default What it does Read more
digits 1 decimal places for a value values
decimal_mark, big_mark ".", "," the marks in a number values
thousands_from 1000 the smallest number that gets a thousands mark values
minus "−" (U+2212) the minus sign values
pct_proportion true whether .pct reads 0.12 as 12% values
count_threshold 10 where .count switches from words to digits values
serial_comma false a comma before the final “and” or “or” of three or more items values
word_limit 100 where .word switches to digits values
date_format "%-d %B %Y" the format of .date values
governor_class ".num" the class that formats the number of an n or sign span values
formatters none project formatters values
ci_level 0.95 the level ci() reports wording
about_tolerance 0.05 how close about() must be wording
sentence_start_fail false fail on a number printed as a numeral at the start of a sentence wording
unit_form "auto" whether units print as symbols or names (auto, symbol, name) units
unit_defaults "weft" si skips the rows of weft’s unit table that redefine a unit the units package already reads, such as pH units
units none units the project defines units
decisions "github" where a dictionary entry’s decision pointer resolves units
bibliography none bibliography files the lints read for citation keys lints
label_words, numeral_years, claim_words, claim_cap, guard_words, expected_names, strict the lints lints
bare_missing true whether a bare value that prints NA, NaN, Inf or -Inf is a warned check values
anchor_calls none helper calls that define anchors for the cross-reference lints lints
severity two patterns regular expressions: a warning or message that matches one fails the render below
ledger true whether a render writes a ledger gate
draft false draft mode gate
verify_skip none parts verify() skips gate
weft_version the version that set the project up; use_weft() maintains it

severity starts with patterns for a singular model fit and a non-positive-definite Hessian. A project adds its own. With severity: ["NAs introduced"], the coercion warning from a laboratory value written “<0.5” stops the render:

Error: weft: 2 failures
  t.Rmd chunk data  [condition]
      warning: NAs introduced by coercion
      matched the severity pattern NAs introduced
  t.Rmd:14  [sentence start] k
      a printed "3" opens a sentence; write .cap (with .count or .word for a number) (rule 5.10.1)

The second failure comes from sentence_start_fail: true, set in the same _weft.yml, for the sentence “`r k` sites were dry.”
